newsitem.title: USA: FCC approves Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger.
newsitem.headline: FCC approves Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday approved the $25.6 billion merger of Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp., sweeping away the last hurdle to the creation of the nation's second-biggest telephone company.
The merger, the biggest in U.S. history, will form the nation's largest local carrier and the No. 2 phone company after long-distance giant AT&T Corp.

The FCC, as expected, attached several conditions to the deal, which is due to close soon. The conditions are meant to ensure the two regional Baby Bell companies open their 13-state market in the Northeast to rivals -- such as AT&T and other long-distance companies -- which want to offer local service. The carriers agreed to the conditions last month, clearing the way for FCC approval.

The Justice Department approved the transaction in April without conditions, infuriating consumer groups while setting the stage for the number of Baby Bells to shrink to five from the original seven after last year's big communications act.

The Telecommunications Act of 1996 tore down barriers to mergers between Baby Bells that had been put in place following the break-up of AT&T in 1984. It also allowed local and long-distance phone companies to do business in each other's markets.
SBC Communications Inc. and Pacific Telesis Group completed a $16.5 billion merger on April 1.
The new Bell Atlantic will serve an area stretching from Maine to Virginia with 39 million phone lines and will rank 23rd on Fortune magazine's list of the nation's 500 largest corporations.
The new company will have more than 140,000 employees offering business and residential customers local, wireless and Internet services.
The companies will have $50 billion in combined assets and are expected soon to seek regulatory approval to offer long-distance calling to customers.
"That's the next move. They've been focused on having to get the merger approved," said Scott Cleland of Legg Mason Precursor Group, research arm of the Baltimore brokerage.
The FCC conditions expire after four years.

As a result of the conditions, Bell Atlantic and Nynex promised to create a uniform electronic system through which rivals can order services and handle installation, billing and other customer-service requirements without delays.
They agreed to offer smaller local phone rivals flexible payment plans for access to the local Bell phone network. That way, small companies are not hit with big up-front payments.
The two companies also agreed to charge new rivals prices based on "forward-looking" costs, rather than "embedded" costs that aim to recoup the cost of previously installed equipment.

The companies also agreed to disclose to the FCC data about their service and the quality of their phone network. Rivals could complain directly to the FCC if they feel that the new Bell Atlantic was not living up to the agreement.

"While we have eliminated the potential that Bell Atlantic will challenge Nynex in the New York City area, we have obtained conditions that will facilitate other competitive entry from Maine to West Virginia," said FCC Commissioner Susan Ness.

MCI Communications Corp. attorney Jonathan Sallet said the terms "will help to alleviate the anti-competitive impact" of the transaction. MCI is among those expected to try to compete with Bell Atlantic for local customers.
But consumer advocates blasted the merger trend among the Bells, saying it hurts phone competition and runs counter to the spirit of the telecom act.
Gene Kimmelman of Consumers Union, a Washington-based group, said the new Bell Atlantic "will have a tremendous advantage" over others.
"I'm fearful that even the long-distance companies will not opt to got head-to-head with such a large company that has a huge advantage over them," he said.
On the New York Stock Exchange, Bell Atlantic rose $1.31 to $75.94. Nynex gained $1.125, to close at $58.06, also on the NYSE.
